description: Ranked search over one public table's rows, with indexed words, prefixes, typos and spelling correction, served from the table's search package. NOT a catalogue search (search_datasets finds datasets) and not SQL. Example: {"table_id": "0f2f...", "query": "blade runner 1982"}. Use the search_table_id from list_tables when the publisher has designated a table for dataset-wide search. The calling agent owns the plan. For a ranking across all matching rows, send query as an empty string and browse with order_by and optional filters. Use a plan for advanced retrieval. Use rerank.ids to select candidates yourself. page_size is 1-100 (default 20). columns is a subset of the table's search display columns (default all of them). Returns {rows: [{row_id, fields}], plan, planner, retrieval, next_cursor, count, package: {generation_id, package_digest}, table_version_id, timings}. For the next page send the same query with the answer's plan and next_cursor. like: a row_id from an answer finds the rows most like that row (more like this; query, when not empty, is a topic beside it), on a table whose search has meaning vectors. mode (first page only): auto (default) looks up the query as a title; meaning ranks by meaning alone; image finds rows whose pictures look like the query (posters showing a red sky over a city); emoji searches by the query's emojis. Most tables search words only. like and the meaning and image modes need meaning vectors, declared by nonempty indexed_plan.semantic_columns (when available) or table.capabilities.search.semantic_columns from get_table_schema. If search_metadata_status is unknown, try the requested indexed mode once. When it is empty, use the default mode. A table whose search cannot run a mode answers invalid_plan. count: true also asks for the exact number of matching rows; count is null when the table cannot count yet. corrected, when present, is the spelling the search used. A table whose search collapses (a passages table that answers for the entities of another table) returns one result per entity: the answer carries collapsed_by (the key column), and each row is the entity's best match with matched_via (up to 8 of its other matching rows, each {row_id, fields}, in ranked order) and group_size (how many of its rows matched in the ranked window). Paging moves over entities. group: "row" asks for every matching row on its own instead; send the same group with a later page. A table whose search does not collapse accepts group and answers ungrouped rows. To point search at a passages table, in this order: declare collapse in its search spec; wait until its search has been rebuilt and is active for that declaration (a newly declared collapse reaches search only after its search build finishes and activates); run one search on that table and confirm the answer carries collapsed_by; only then set search_table_id. If the answer does not carry collapsed_by, do not set search_table_id. Find the table with search_datasets and list_tables. get_table_schema returns table.capabilities.search for a declared index. If search_metadata_status is unknown, metadata could not be confirmed; one indexed search can check. Its state says whether search_table answers now. ready means it answers. preparing means a package is being built, and search may still answer from the previous version's package, so try it. unavailable means no package and no build. No state means Cloud has not read it yet, or the table is a recorded stream, whose state Cloud never reads, so try it. A refused search answers search_unavailable with a reason and retry_after_seconds. preparing means the search package is being built or loaded, and service_unavailable means the search service is down. For both, wait retry_after_seconds and retry once. build_failed means the package failed to build, no_package means the table has no search package, not_servable means the table's search package cannot be served right now, and not_public means another workspace's private or link-shared table. For these four, retry_after_seconds is null and retrying will not help, so use query_table or sample_rows instead. Your own workspace's tables are searchable whatever their visibility. For a published table in the inventory, use search_table first to find a record by name or title, even with a date or another qualifier, unless the index is known to be unavailable. Send the name as query, use a small page_size and presentation answer for a requested record. Verify its qualifiers in the returned fields. For conceptual similarity use the semantic index when supported. For newest, oldest, highest, lowest, best-rated or other top rows across a published table, start with search_table using query as an empty string, browse.order_by for the metric and browse.filters for requested constraints. Omit columns for ranked cards to use the published display fields. Filtering and sorting do not require returning those fields. Use the applied plan to verify the filter and order. The entity named in the question defines the population. When a table mixes entity types, apply the requested type as a filter before ordering and limiting, even if the user did not phrase it as a filter. Check the schema if the discriminator or its value is unclear. Match each required condition to a field with that meaning. Keep every required condition when switching tools. A correlated field is a different question and requires the user’s agreement. Keep candidate pages in work history until every condition is verified and the requested ordering covers the matching population. If an exact answer is unavailable, say which condition you could not verify and omit the answer widget. Use the listed ready filterable_columns and sortable_columns. If the inventory omits a requested field, inspect get_table_schema before choosing a scan, declaring a condition unsupported, or asking the user to change it. Use the field that represents the requested relationship. When a table’s search entry says sortable_complete, its sortable_columns are every column the index can order by with a plain column and direction: to order that way by any other column, use query_table directly and do not try the index first. The filter list may be partial. If a required field exists in the schema but is missing from a ready index’s filter list, try one indexed browse with the exact predicate before a scan. Check the returned plan for unresolved conditions and verify the ordering. A declared index is a hint; missing inventory metadata is unknown. Read get_table_schema only for missing capabilities needed by the operation. Use query_table for aggregates, calculations, unsupported filters or ordering, or when lookup reports no usable index. Respect access and budget errors. Consult table.capabilities.search.indexed_plan for advanced plans or when the direct lookup needs refinement. For projection use only declared display_columns, or omit columns for defaults. Use mode or like on a first page; an explicit plan carries its own mode. If refused, check detail and diagnostics, correct the named field and retry only when the request has changed. Use title lookup for names and misspellings. For topics, use a description plan for keyword and embedding retrieval, or meaning mode for paraphrases. Split explicit constraints into predicates on filterable_columns and requested ordering into order on sortable_columns. Keep residual topic words in text. Put optional preferences in prefer only for supported values. For filtered catalog-wide ordering use browse with an empty query; the tool builds the matching_rows plan. A description plan orders a relevance_window only. Use query_table for aggregates or unsupported exact operations. Report the returned scope, and respect refusals. Set predicate and order origin to explicit for requested constraints. No key needed on a public table: a keyless caller gets 30 calls a minute and 600 a day per address, and 300 a minute and 10,000 a day across all keyless callers, and settled calls share the dataset page's per-table limit. A refusal past that answers rate_limited with retry_after_seconds. Without a key, private and link-shared tables, and public tables whose publisher turned download off, answer table_not_available. An mr_use_ workspace key (Authorization: Bearer) or an OAuth connection lifts the limit to the key's query limit (60 calls a minute per key or connection, shared with query_table, and 5,000 a day per workspace, with no daily limit on the paid plan) and adds the workspace's own tables. A keyed call counts against the workspace's allowance, as query_table does. Cite the package generation and digest.

browse.description: Whole-table indexed filtering and ranking. Send query as an empty string. Use published filterable and sortable columns.
